name: Transformation Efficiency Calculator
seoDesc: Transformation efficiency is the number of transformants per microgram of plasmid — the number that tells you whether your competent cells are any good. Free
summary:
Transformation efficiency is the number of transformants per microgram of plasmid — the number that tells you whether your competent cells are any good. It returns transformation efficiency, total transformants and transformants per ng, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator computes it from colonies, plated volume and plasmid mass, and flags the values that mean something went wrong. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Transformation Efficiency
sections.html:
Efficiency (CFU/µg) = colonies × (recovery volume ÷ plated volume) × dilution ÷ µg DNA

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
coloniescolonies on the countable plateCFU
recoveryvolume the cells were resuspended inmL
volume platedfraction of the recovery that was platedmL
dnamass of plasmid addedng

sections.title: How do I use the Transformation Efficiency?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: colonies on the plate of 320 CFU, volume plated of 0.1 mL, recovery volume of 1 mL, plasmid dna transformed of 10 ng, dilution plated of 1 ×.

Substituting them into the formula gives transformation efficiency of 320,000 CFU/µg, total transformants of 3,200 CFU, transformants per ng of 320 CFU/ng.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
above 1 × 10⁸Excellentchemically competent commercial-grade cells
1 × 10⁷ – 1 × 10⁸Goodfine for cloning and library work
1 × 10⁶ – 1 × 10⁷Adequatecheck heat shock, antibiotics and DNA quality
below 1 × 10⁶Poorusually competent-cell preparation or a salt problem

  • Efficiency drops sharply with plasmid size: a 10 kb construct transforms several times less well than a 3 kb one, and that is not a competent-cell problem.

  • Plate a range of volumes (10 µL and 100 µL of the recovery) so at least one plate is countable.

  • The antibiotic must be at the right concentration and the plates fresh; old ampicillin plates give satellite colonies that look like transformants.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Using the plated volume as if it were the whole recovery.
  • Reporting CFU/µg using the mass of DNA in the ligation rather than the plasmid transformed.
  • Reading efficiency from a plate with 2000 colonies, where the count is meaningless.

faq.q: What is a good transformation efficiency?
faq.a: 10⁸ CFU/µg or better for chemically competent cells; 10⁹–10¹⁰ for electroporation.

faq.q: Why is my efficiency low for a ligation?
faq.a: Ligations contain nicked and linear DNA; efficiency is quoted for supercoiled plasmid.

faq.q: What does the Transformation Efficiency actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns transformation efficiency, total transformants and transformants per ng. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
